evidence: The model may generate videos without motion, or very slow camera pans.
value: Vendor states the model may produce a near-static clip: no motion at all, or only a very slow camera pan. A generation that comes back frozen is expected behaviour, not a bad seed.

evidence: The model cannot be controlled through text.
value: No text conditioning at all — the clip cannot be steered by a prompt, only by the conditioning image. Any workflow that expects prompt control over SVD output is mis-specified.

evidence: Faces and people in general may not be generated properly.
value: Vendor explicitly flags people and faces as a weak class — disqualifying for talking-head / lipsync work built on SVD.

evidence: The model cannot render legible text.
value: Cannot render legible text; and the autoencoder itself is lossy, so degradation is present even before the diffusion stage is blamed.

evidence: The autoencoding part of the model is lossy.
value: Reconstruction loss is architectural: the VAE round-trip is lossy, so fine detail in the conditioning image will not survive to the output frames.

evidence: The generated videos are rather short (<= 4sec), and the model does not achieve perfect photorealism.
value: Ceiling of ~4 seconds and photorealism is explicitly not achieved. XT variant is 25 frames at 576x1024 — a hard budget, not a tunable.

evidence: The model was not trained to be factual or true representations of people or events, and therefore using the model to generate such content is out-of-scope for the abilities of this model.
value: Vendor declares likeness/event fidelity out of scope — so using SVD to animate a real person's photo is outside stated model ability, independent of policy.

evidence: In some edge cases with extreme motion, minor warping and distortions can also occur.
fix: Keep motion moderate; the card frames this as an edge-case regime, so authoring lower-amplitude motion avoids it.
value: Fast or large motion is the named failure trigger: warping and distortion appear at motion extremes.

evidence: Prompt following is heavily influenced by the prompting-style.
fix: Card's own prescription is long, elaborate English prose: "Prompts should be in English. The more elaborate the better."
value: Prompt adherence is explicitly imperfect AND style-sensitive: the same semantic request phrased differently gives different adherence. Prompt style is a first-order variable for LTX, not a polish step.

evidence: The model works best on resolutions under 720 x 1280 and number of frames below 257.
fix: Choose resolution divisible by 32 and frames divisible by 8 plus 1 (e.g. 257) so no padding/cropping occurs.
value: Quality falls off outside a stated operating window: above 720x1280 or past 257 frames. Also hard-constrained to resolutions divisible by 32 and frame counts of 8n+1 — off-grid inputs are padded with -1 and cropped, which is a silent quality tax rather than an error.

evidence: This model is not intended or able to provide factual information.
value: Vendor disclaims factual grounding outright — LTX output should never be treated as depicting anything real.

evidence: 720 x 480, no support for other resolutions (including fine-tuning)
value: Resolution is frozen at 720x480 and the card states fine-tuning cannot change it. Any other aspect ratio requires external crop/upscale.

evidence: Prompt Length Limit 226 Tokens
value: Hard prompt budget of 226 tokens — long cinematic prompts are truncated, so detail placed late in a prompt is silently dropped. Fixed 6 s at 8 fps.

evidence: The model only supports English input; other languages can be translated into English during refinement by a large model.
value: English-only text encoder. Non-English prompts must be machine-translated first, which introduces a paraphrase step between author intent and the model.

evidence: Please note that the evaluation is based on Hunyuan Video's high-quality version. This is different from the currently released fast version.
value: The human-eval table (61.8% text alignment, 66.5% motion quality, 95.7% visual quality, rank 1 over Gen-3/Luma) was NOT measured on the weights you can download. Vendor says the scored model is a different, high-quality version than the released fast version — so the published win over Gen-3 does not transfer to the open checkpoint.

evidence: The Master mode enhances the description of aspects such as composition, lighting, and camera movement, which leans towards generating videos with a higher visual quality. However, this emphasis may occasionally result in the loss of some semantic details.
fix: Use Normal mode when intent fidelity matters: it "is designed to enhance the video generation model's comprehension of user intent".
value: Their own prompt-rewrite Master mode trades semantics for looks: it improves composition/lighting/camera but drops meaning. For a scripted shot where content matters, Master mode is the wrong setting.

evidence: (3) Tests were run without the --use_prompt_extend flag;
value: The published efficiency table was measured with prompt extension OFF, while the same card recommends running WITH prompt extension. So the quoted times/memory understate the real pipeline cost, and the quality the card advertises comes from a config the benchmark did not run.

evidence: Extending the prompts can effectively enrich the details in the generated videos, further enhancing the video quality. Therefore, we recommend enabling prompt extension.
fix: Run --use_prompt_extend (dashscope or local Qwen); card notes "Larger models generally provide better extension results but require more GPU memory."
value: Vendor treats the raw prompt as insufficient: an LLM rewrite step is the recommended path to the advertised detail level. Bare user prompts are the degraded mode.

evidence: Without setting --num_clip, the generated video length will automatically adjust based on the input audio length
fix: Use --pose_video to constrain body motion: "The --pose_video parameter enables pose-driven generation, allowing the model to follow specific pose sequences while generating videos synchronized with audio input."
value: Clip length is driven by audio duration, not a duration parameter — long takes are produced as chained clips (--num_clip), which is the seam where long-form drift shows up. Pose conditioning (--pose_video) is the separate lever for body motion.

evidence: The model may fail to generate output that matches the prompts. Prompt following is heavily influenced by the prompting-style.
fix: Treat prompt phrasing style as a tuned parameter, not a neutral carrier; hold wording fixed when comparing seeds.
value: Vendor states outright that the model may not render the prompt: prompt adherence is not guaranteed and is style-dependent, so identical semantic content phrased differently gives different adherence. Identical wording appears verbatim on the FLUX.1-schnell and FLUX.1-Krea-dev cards.

evidence: This model is not intended or able to provide factual information.
value: Not usable for anything requiring factual correctness about the world (real people, real places, real products, diagrams that must be true).

evidence: While this model can handle long prompts, you may observe artifacts on the edge of generations when T5 tokens go over 256. Pay attention to the token limits when using this model in your workflow, and shortern prompts if artifacts becomes too obvious.
fix: Count T5 tokens and keep under 256; shorten the prompt when edge artifacts become obvious.
value: Prompt exceeds 256 T5 tokens: visible artifacts appear specifically at the EDGES of the generation, not distributed across it. A long prompt therefore fails in a way that is easy to miss on a centre-cropped preview.

evidence: The medium model has a different training data distribution than the large model, so it may not respond to the same prompt similarly.
fix: Re-tune prompts per checkpoint; do not carry a Large-tuned prompt set to Medium unchanged.
value: Prompts are NOT portable between SD3.5 Medium and SD3.5 Large — different training data distribution means the same prompt can produce a materially different response. A prompt library tuned on Large does not transfer.

evidence: We recommend sampling with Skip Layer Guidance for better structure and anatomy coherency.
fix: Sample with Skip Layer Guidance.
value: Structure and anatomy coherency is weak under plain sampling — the vendor's own recommended default is Skip Layer Guidance, which is an admission that bodies/limbs come out incoherent without it.

evidence: The model was not trained to be factual or true representations of people or events. As such, using the model to generate such content is out-of-scope of the abilities of this model.
value: Explicitly out of scope for true representations of people or events — i.e. likeness of a real person is not a supported use, not merely a policy restriction but a stated ability gap.

evidence: Figure 15 : Editing failure cases. Top row: An example for identity degradation: While the center image shows a good edit, preserving character identity the right one (using a slightly modified prompt) comes with significant identity loss. Middle row: Scene modification instead of object movement: the model adds milk foam rather than repositioning the mug. Bottom row: After six iterative edits, samples can exhibit visible artifacts.
value: Six iterative edits is the observed threshold at which artifacts become visible, and identity loss can be triggered by a SLIGHT prompt change on an otherwise-good edit; the model also substitutes a scene change for a requested object move (adds milk foam instead of repositioning the mug).

evidence: The model occasionally fails to follow instructions accurately, ignoring specific prompt requirements. In addition, the distillation process can introduce visual artifacts that impact the fidelity of the output.
value: Instruction-following is not reliable at the level of individual prompt clauses — specific requirements get silently dropped; separately, the guidance-distillation used to make it fast is itself a named source of fidelity-damaging artifacts.

evidence: We additionally compute the cosine similarity of AuraFace [ 10 , 22 ] embeddings between the input and images generated via successive edits, highlighting the slower drift of FLUX.1 Kontext relative to competing methods.
fix: Instrument your own edit chain with AuraFace (huggingface.co/fal/AuraFace-v1) embedding cosine similarity and set a stop threshold.
value: BFL's own way of measuring identity retention is cosine similarity of AuraFace face embeddings between the input image and each successive edit — a reproducible instrument for the drift above, not a human eyeball call.

evidence: We observe that FLUX.1 Kontext [Pro] struggles with consistency when editing non-photorealistic images, while both SeedEdit 3.0 and Qwen-Image produce coherent results that align well with the desired cartoon style.
value: Editing NON-photorealistic source images (cartoon/illustration) breaks consistency — competitor-reported, so treat as НЕПРОВЕРЕНО until reproduced, but it is a specific and testable claim.

evidence: This benchmark contains 2K prompts, each requiring 2–5 regions of English to be rendered on the generated image. ... FLUX.1 [dev] ( BlackForest, 2024 ) 0.6089 0.5531 0.4661 0.4316 0.4965
fix: Composite multi-region text in post rather than asking one generation for 4-5 text areas.
value: English text rendering collapses as the number of distinct text REGIONS in one image grows: CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.6089 at 2 regions -> 0.5531 at 3 -> 0.4661 at 4 -> 0.4316 at 5 (average 0.4965). Under half the words are right once a layout has 5 text areas.

Same region-count degradation, milder: CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.7293 (2 regions) -> 0.6825 -> 0.6574 -> 0.5940 (5 regions), average 0.6548. Better than FLUX.1-dev at every region count but still loses ~13 points from 2 to 5 regions.

evidence: HiDream-I1-Full ( Cai et al., 2025 ) 0.543 0.024 FLUX.1 [Dev] ( BlackForest, 2024 ) 0.607 0.005
fix: Do not attempt CJK typography in FLUX/HiDream; use Qwen-Image (0.946 ZH) or overlay the type.
value: Chinese long-text rendering is effectively zero: LongText-Bench-ZH 0.005 against 0.607 on the English split. HiDream-I1-Full is the same story (0.543 EN / 0.024 ZH). Western open-weight models are English-only for legible text in practice.

evidence: Table 9: Quantitative comparison results of Chinese text rendering. ... Qwen-Image 97.29 40.53 6.48 58.30
fix: Restrict generated Chinese text to Level-1 common characters; render anything rarer as an overlay.
value: Even the Chinese-text leader falls apart on rare characters: ChineseWord accuracy 97.29 on Level-1 (3500 common chars), 40.53 on Level-2, 6.48 on Level-3 (1605 rare chars). Character frequency, not language, is the real axis of failure — GPT Image 1 [High] scores 3.55 and Seedream 3.0 1.25 at Level-3.

fix: Never trust an overall GenEval number as an applicability signal; read Position and Color-attribution subscores.
value: GenEval exposes compositional weakness where the overall score hides it: overall 0.66, but Position 0.22 and Color attribution 0.45 while Single Object is 0.98. Spatial relations ('X to the left of Y') and per-object colour binding are where prompts break, not object rendering.

evidence: The original Qwen-Image struggles to accurately render aged facial features (e.g., wrinkles), resulting in an artificial “AI look.” In contrast, Qwen-Image-2512 precisely captures age cues, dramatically boosting realism.
fix: Use Qwen-Image-2512 (Dec 2025) rather than the original Aug 2025 weights for human realism, hair detail and pose adherence.
value: Vendor's own before/after write-up names three concrete weaknesses of the August 2025 Qwen-Image release, fixed only in the December 2512 checkpoint: elderly faces come out smoothed with an artificial 'AI look', hair strands blur together into a mass, and posture instructions ('body leaning slightly forward') are not obeyed.

evidence: Due to limited model size (6B parameters), Z-Image exhibits limitations in world knowledge, intent understanding, and complex reasoning. However, it serves as a powerful text decoder capable of translating detailed prompts into realistic images.
fix: Front it with a VLM Prompt Enhancer (the vendor's own remedy) and feed it fully-specified prompts.
value: The 6B parameter count buys the 16GB-VRAM footprint at the cost of world knowledge, intent understanding and complex reasoning — the model is a strong renderer of already-explicit prompts, not an interpreter of terse or knowledge-laden ones.

evidence: The Pretrain Checkpoint does not automatically rewrite or enhance input prompts, for optimal results currently, we recommend community partners to use deepseek to rewrite the prompts.
fix: Run an LLM prompt-rewrite stage in front of the base checkpoint, or use HunyuanImage-3.0-Instruct which self-rewrites.
value: The base/pretrain checkpoint does not rewrite or enhance prompts and does not perform acceptably without an EXTERNAL LLM rewriting the prompt first — the vendor names DeepSeek. Only the -Instruct variants have prompt self-rewrite.
VBench-2.0 Human Identity 71.95%, Human Anatomy 86.99%, Human Clothes 91.75% — identity is the weakest of its three human dimensions despite strong VBench-1.0 subject consistency (98.33%).
VBench-2.0 Human Identity 75.67%, Human Anatomy 88.58% (best anatomy of the four), Human Clothes 82.97% (worst clothes) — strong on human content, weak on most other VBench-2.0 dimensions.

evidence: Training data used by the authors of the AnimateDiff paper contained Shutterstock watermarks. Since mm_sd_v15 was finetuned on finer, less drastic movement, the motion module attempts to replicate the transparency of that watermark and does not get blurred away like mm_sd_v14.
fix: Use other motion modules, or combine them via Advanced KSamplers.
value: Visible Shutterstock watermark bleeds into output because the motion module reproduces the training-data watermark; mm_sd_v14 blurs it away, mm_sd_v15 does not.

evidence: NOTE: You will need to use ```autoselect``` or ```linear (HotshotXL/default)``` beta_schedule, the sweetspot for context_length or total frames (when not using context) is 8 frames, and you will need to use an SDXL checkpoint.
fix: Use autoselect or linear (HotshotXL/default) beta_schedule and an SDXL checkpoint.
value: Coherent clip length is ~8 frames; beyond that you must use sliding context windows, and 8 is the stated sweet spot for total frames without context.

evidence: Caveat: the original loras really only work on v2-based motion models like ```mm_sd_v15_v2```, ```mm-p_0.5.pth```, and ```mm-p_0.75.pth```.
fix: Train replacement motion LoRAs without the v2 limitation via the AnimateDiff-MotionDirector repo.
value: The original AnimateDiff motion LoRAs only take effect on v2-based motion models; applied to v1/v3 modules they are effectively inert.

evidence: While this was intended as an img2video model, I found it works best for vid2vid purposes with ```ref_drift=0.0```, and to use it for only at least 1 step before switching over to other models via chaining with toher Apply AnimateDiff Model (Adv.) nodes.
fix: Set ref_drift=0.0, use it for at least 1 step, then chain to other Apply AnimateDiff Model (Adv.) nodes.
value: Despite being trained and released as an image-to-video model, in practice it performs best used for vid2vid, and only for a step or so before chaining to another motion model.

evidence: AnimateLCM-I2V is also extremely useful for maintaining coherence at higher resolutions (with ControlNet and SD LoRAs active, I could easily upscale from 512x512 source to 1024x1024 in a single pass).
value: Reported as the practical tool for holding coherence when upscaling video resolution, 512x512 source to 1024x1024 in one pass with ControlNet and SD LoRAs active.

evidence: [AnimateDiff-SDXL](https://github.com/guoyww/AnimateDiff/) support, with corresponding model. Still in beta after several months.
value: The SDXL motion module never reached production quality; the maintainer still labels it beta many months after release.

evidence: NOTE: Requires AnimateDiff SD1.5 models, and was specifically trained for v3 model.
value: Camera control conditioning is tied to a specific base: it only works with AnimateDiff SD1.5 motion models and was trained specifically for the v3 module, so it does not transfer to SDXL or other video bases.

evidence: augmentation level: The amount of noise added to the init image, the higher it is the less the video will look like the init image. Increase it for more motion.
value: Motion and fidelity to the input image trade off directly against each other through augmentation_level: buying more motion costs likeness to the init frame.

evidence: In the above example the first frame will be cfg 1.0 (the min_cfg in the node) the middle frame 1.75 and the last frame 2.5. (the cfg set in the sampler). This way frames further away from the init frame get a gradually higher cfg.
fix: Use VideoLinearCFGGuidance to ramp cfg from min_cfg on the first frame to the sampler cfg on the last.
value: Sampling quality is not uniform across the clip: frames further from the init frame need progressively stronger guidance, which is why a linearly ramped CFG across frames improves results over a flat CFG.

evidence: [ip-adapter-full-face_sd15.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/h94/IP-Adapter/resolve/main/models/ip-adapter-full-face_sd15.safetensors), Stronger face model, not necessarily better
value: The stronger full-face identity adapter is not the better choice by default; more identity strength does not mean a better result.

evidence: Usually it's a good idea to lower the `weight` to at least `0.8` and increase the number steps. To increase adherece to the prompt you may try to change the **weight type** in the `IPAdapter Advanced` node.
fix: Lower weight to at least 0.8, increase steps, and change the weight type in IPAdapter Advanced to recover prompt adherence.
value: At full weight the reference image overrides prompt adherence; the maintained default advice is to run below 1.0 and add steps.

evidence: The model generally follows instructions more reliably in shorter clips. For best results, aim for concise shots. If your project allows, you may see better results by stitching together two 4 second clips in editing instead of generating a single 8 second clip.
fix: Generate concise shots and stitch in edit instead of asking for one longer clip.
value: Instruction following degrades as clip length grows; OpenAI recommends stitching two 4-second clips rather than generating one 8-second clip.

evidence: You should also think about rhythm and timing: a 4-second shot will usually accommodate one or two short exchanges, while an 8-second clip can support a few more. Long, complex speeches are unlikely to sync well and may break pacing.
fix: Keep dialogue to a handful of short lines budgeted to the clip length; label speakers consistently and alternate turns.
value: Long or complex spoken lines do not lip-sync and break pacing; a 4s shot holds only one or two short exchanges, an 8s clip a few more.

evidence: When introducing characters, expect some unpredictability—small changes in phrasing can alter identity, pose, or the focus of the scene itself. Keep descriptions consistent across shots, reuse phrasing for continuity, and avoid mixing traits that may compete.
fix: Keep descriptions consistent across shots, reuse the same phrasing, avoid competing traits.
value: Character identity is phrasing-sensitive: small wording changes across shots can change identity, pose or scene focus.

evidence: Video resolution directly influences visual fidelity and motion consistency in Sora. Higher resolutions generate detail, texture, and lighting transitions more accurately, while lower resolutions compress visual information, often introducing softness or artifacts.
fix: Use sora-2-pro at 1920x1080 / 1080x1920 when motion consistency matters.
value: Lower resolutions compress visual information and introduce softness or artifacts; motion consistency is resolution-dependent, not just fidelity.

evidence: Character uploads that depict human likeness are blocked by default. Contact your account manager or reach out to our sales team to learn more about eligibility for human-likeness access.
fix: Contact account manager / sales for human-likeness access; otherwise characters are limited to animals and objects.
value: Human likeness is out of scope for the Characters API: human-likeness character uploads are blocked by default and require account-manager eligibility.

evidence: Real people—including public figures—cannot be generated. Character uploads that depict human likeness are blocked by default. Input images with faces of humans are currently rejected.
value: Any input image containing a human face is rejected, and real people including public figures cannot be generated — a hard block on face-driven lipsync workflows.

evidence: Character uploads currently work best with short 2 - to 4 -second clips in 16:9 or 9:16 , at 720p to 1080p . Character source videos work best when they match the aspect ratio of the requested output. If the aspect ratios differ, the character can appear stretched or distorted.
fix: Match the character clip's aspect ratio to the requested output size.
value: Character source video whose aspect ratio differs from the requested output produces a stretched or distorted character; characters work best on 2–4s, 16:9 or 9:16, 720p–1080p sources.

evidence: Mention the character name verbatim in your prompt. Passing the character ID alone isn’t enough to reliably preserve the character in the shot.
fix: Mention the character name verbatim in the prompt.
value: Passing a character ID without naming the character in the prompt text does not reliably preserve the character — the ID alone is insufficient conditioning.

evidence: Extensions currently accept only a source video and prompt. They don’t support characters or image references.
value: Extensions are mutually exclusive with the identity-preservation features: they accept only a source video and prompt, no characters and no image references.

evidence: Each extension can add up to 20 seconds. A single video can be extended up to six times, for a maximum total length of 120 seconds.
value: Maximum total clip length is 120 seconds, reached only via at most six extensions of up to 20 seconds each.

evidence: The image must match the target video’s resolution ( size ). Supported file formats are image/jpeg , image/png , and image/webp .
value: An input_reference image must exactly match the target video resolution, and only jpeg/png/webp are accepted; it conditions only the first frame.

evidence: This works best when you make a single, well-defined change because smaller, focused edits preserve more of the original fidelity and reduce the risk of introducing artifacts.
fix: Constrain each edit to a single well-defined change; if a shot keeps misfiring, freeze the camera, simplify the action, clear the background, then re-layer complexity.
value: Video edits introduce artifacts and lose original fidelity when more than one change is requested at a time.

evidence: Treat your prompt as a creative wish list, not a contract. Like with ChatGPT, using the same prompt multiple times will lead to different results – this is a feature, not a bug.
fix: Treat the prompt as a wish list, not a contract; sample several takes before judging.
value: Generation is non-deterministic by design — identical prompts yield different takes, so a single render is not evidence about a prompt.

evidence: These parameters are the video’s container: resolution, duration, and character references will not change based on prose like “make it longer.” Set them explicitly in the API call; your prompt controls everything else (subject, motion, lighting, style).
fix: Set size, seconds and characters explicitly in the API call.
value: Resolution, duration and character references are container parameters the prompt cannot influence — prose like "make it longer" is ignored.

evidence: Longer durations and 1080p jobs can take materially longer to complete than short 720p or 480p renders, so plan for higher latency in user-facing flows.
fix: Plan for higher latency in user-facing flows; iterate at short/low resolution.
value: Longer durations and 1080p jobs take materially longer than 720p/480p renders; a single render may take several minutes.

evidence: Download URLs are valid for a maximum of 1 hour after generation. If you need long-term storage, copy the file to your own storage system promptly.
fix: Copy the MP4 to your own storage immediately after completion.
value: Generated output is ephemeral: download URLs expire after 1 hour (24 hours for Batch-produced videos).

evidence: The Sora 2 video generation models and Videos API are deprecated and will shut down on September 24, 2026. This affects Videos API, sora-2 , sora-2-pro , sora-2-2025-10-06 , sora-2-2025-12-08 , and sora-2-pro-2025-10-06 .
value: The whole Sora 2 family and the Videos API are deprecated with a shutdown date of September 24, 2026 — a planning constraint for any pipeline built on it.

evidence: Only content suitable for audiences under 18 (a setting to bypass this restriction will be available in the future). Copyrighted characters and copyrighted music will be rejected.
value: API-wide content restriction: only under-18-suitable content, and copyrighted characters or music are rejected outright.

evidence: Text Rendering: Although significantly improved, the model can still struggle with precise text placement and clarity.
value: Text rendering still fails on precise placement and clarity, despite improvement.

evidence: Consistency: While capable of producing consistent imagery, the model may occasionally struggle to maintain visual consistency for recurring characters or brand elements across multiple generations.
value: Visual consistency for recurring characters or brand elements across multiple generations is not guaranteed — OpenAI's own stated limitation.

evidence: Composition Control: Despite improved instruction following, the model may have difficulty placing elements precisely in structured or layout-sensitive compositions.
value: Precise element placement in structured or layout-sensitive compositions is unreliable; complex prompts can take up to 2 minutes.

evidence: Masking with GPT Image is entirely prompt-based. The model uses the mask as guidance, but may not follow its exact shape with complete precision.
value: Masked edits are prompt-based only: the mask is guidance and the model may not respect its exact shape, so it is not a hard inpainting boundary. With multiple input images the mask applies only to the first.

evidence: Some image generation failures are user-correctable and may return error.type = "image_generation_user_error" . Don’t automatically retry these errors without modifying the prompt or input images.
fix: Branch on error.code = "moderation_blocked" and use moderation_details.moderation_stage to decide whether to revise the prompt or log an output-side block; never retry without changing the request.
value: Moderation blocks are labelled by stage — input (prompt/inputs), output (generated image), or unknown — under error.code = moderation_blocked, and these are user errors that must not be auto-retried.

evidence: A quoted line without a visible speaker or a voiceover cue may be treated as text that belongs in the frame. Make the distinction explicit when it matters.
fix: Name a visible speaker or say `voiceover`, keep the exact line in quotes, and add `no on-screen text or subtitles`
value: A quoted line of dialogue with no visible speaker and no voiceover cue can be rendered as on-screen text instead of spoken audio

evidence: If speech is the focus, keep other voices out of the background. Crowd conversation, a talking radio, or another narrator can compete with the main line. Weather, machinery, footsteps, and traffic are easier to layer under speech because they do not introduce more words.
fix: Troubleshooting table: "The words become garbled — Remove competing speech such as crowd conversation, a talking radio, or a second voice"
value: Speech becomes garbled when other speech (crowd, radio, second voice) is in the mix; non-verbal ambience does not cause this

evidence: A short line in a longer clip is safer than copy written to fill every second. If the final word gets cut off, shorten the line or increase the clip duration. Timing instructions can give the model a target, but they are not exact
fix: Shorten the line, raise the duration, or ask for the line to finish earlier
value: The final word of a line can be cut off when the script is written to fill the clip duration; timing directives are approximate, not exact

evidence: Language, accent, line order, speaker attribution, and timing are directable targets rather than exact controls. Review each take by ear when the performance matters.
value: Language, accent, line order, speaker attribution and timing are directable targets, not controls — every take needs an ear check

evidence: This can preserve the same kind of voice, but it does not guarantee the same performer on every generation. Treat the prompt as casting direction rather than a fixed speaker identity.
fix: Reuse the full voice direction (person, register, recording setup, delivery) and compare takes by ear before cutting them into one sequence
value: Voice identity does not persist across generations: identical voice direction reproduces a kind of voice, not the same performer

evidence: Multi-speaker attribution and interruptions are still review-heavy. Name each speaker, keep turns short, and judge each take by ear before relying on who said what.
fix: Split the scene: "Do not force several speakers, a long script, and multiple visual beats into a short clip."
value: Multi-speaker attribution and interruptions are unreliable — who said what cannot be relied on without review

evidence: Name the sound source you want rather than asking for silence. `Rain against the window` or `a soft piano bed` gives the model something concrete; `quiet room tone` may collapse into static or dead air.
value: Asking for silence/quiet backfires: an absence-of-sound request can render as static or dead air

evidence: Use only the details that change the read. Long stacks of personality adjectives can fight each other. Directions such as `one audible breath` can also make that breath too prominent.
value: Stacked personality adjectives fight each other and micro-direction over-renders: asking for one breath makes the breath too prominent

evidence: Phrases such as `professional, warm, and engaging` leave most of the voice to the model. They often produce the same polished read: careful diction, even pauses, and more energy than the scene needs.
fix: Troubleshooting: "The cadence is sing-song — Simplify punctuation, remove repetitive sentence shapes, and ask for a relaxed conversational rhythm"
value: Generic voice adjectives collapse to one house read; punctuation-heavy copy produces sing-song cadence

evidence: **Subject description** — a fixed description held identically across shots, so identity stays consistent.
value: Visual identity across shots is held only by re-stating a fixed subject description verbatim in every shot

evidence: Order matters: the frames are read as a timeline from first to last. Space them so each transition is achievable, and keep the look consistent across frames so the shot reads as one take rather than a series of cuts.
value: Keyframes read strictly as a timeline; inconsistent looks between frames make the output read as cuts rather than one take

evidence: Important: You can't disable the prompt rewriter when using Veo 3 and 3.1 models.
value: The prompt you send is not the prompt that runs: the LLM prompt rewriter cannot be disabled on Veo 3 and 3.1

evidence: A rewritten prompt is delivered by API response only if the original prompt is fewer than 30 words long.
value: The rewritten prompt is only returned when the original is under 30 words, so long production prompts run through an unobservable rewrite

evidence: Rejects requests to generate a photorealistic representation of a prominent person or if the project isn't on the allowlist for this feature.
fix: Read the numeric support code in the output to identify the category; child-depicting content likewise requires personGeneration set to "allow_all" or an allowlist
value: Photorealistic renditions of a prominent person are rejected outright (support codes 29310472 / 15236754) unless the project is allowlisted

evidence: If fewer videos than requested are returned, then some generated output is being blocked for not meeting safety requirements.
fix: Count returned samples against the requested count rather than checking only for an error message
value: Safety blocking is partly silent: a short count of returned videos, not an error, is the only signal that outputs were blocked

evidence: we demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models are highly susceptible to meaning-preserving perturbations, which significantly degrade contextual faithfulness (by up to 50% for GPT-5-mini).
fix: Stress-test a RAG deployment with paraphrases of the same query, not just the canonical phrasing; a single-phrasing faithfulness score is not a deployment guarantee.
value: Contextual faithfulness in RAG collapses under meaning-preserving query rewrites: adversarially optimized but semantically equivalent user queries degrade GPT-5-mini's grounding by up to 50% (COLM 2026, posted 2026-08-04, 5 open + 5 closed models, 3 datasets).

evidence: Across four representative state-of-the-art frameworks, replacing GPT-5 with Qwen3.5-9B reduces average OSWorld SR-100 from 60.9\% to 37.7\%. Trajectory annotation further identifies at least one control failure in 91.6\% of failed trajectories.
value: OSWorld SR-100 averaged across four state-of-the-art GUI-agent frameworks (posted 2026-08-26): GPT-5 as planner backbone reaches 60.9%; swapping in Qwen3.5-9B drops it to 37.7%. At least one control failure was annotated in 91.6% of failed trajectories.

evidence: Many people have reported that the teeth and lips generated by LatentSync 1.5 are blurry. To address this issue, we trained LatentSync 1.6 on 512 x 512 resolution videos.
fix: Use LatentSync 1.6 checkpoint and set the `resolution` parameter in the U-Net config to 512.
value: Teeth and lips render blurry at the 256x256 training resolution; ByteDance retrained at 512x512 as LatentSync 1.6 specifically to fix it. Nothing else in the model changed.

evidence: `guidance_scale` [1.0-3.0]: A higher value improves lip-sync accuracy but may cause the video distortion or jitter.
fix: Stay inside the stated range; trade against inference_steps [20-50] which raises quality at the cost of speed.
value: Raising guidance_scale to buy lip-sync accuracy costs visual stability: the vendor names distortion and jitter as the consequence. Usable band is 1.0-3.0.

evidence: Split each video into 5-10 second segments.
fix: Resample source to 25 fps and 16 kHz audio, cut at scene boundaries, before inference.
value: Trained exclusively on 5-10 second clips, 25 fps, faces affine-warped to a fixed crop, filtered to SyncNet confidence >=3 and hyperIQA >=40. Input outside that envelope (long single shots, other frame rates, low-IQ source) is out of distribution.

evidence: Note that our released SyncNet is trained on data processed through our data processing pipeline, which includes special operations such as affine transformation and audio-visual adjustment. Therefore, before evaluation, the test data must first be processed using the provided pipeline.
fix: Run the provided data_processing_pipeline.sh on any test set before scoring with their SyncNet.
value: The released StableSyncNet (94% accuracy) is only valid as a scorer on data run through LatentSync's own preprocessing (affine transform + audio-visual offset zeroing). Sync-confidence numbers computed on raw video are not comparable.

evidence: Our previous claim that the [temporal layer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04725) severely impairs lip-sync accuracy was incorrect; the issue was actually caused by a bug in the code implementation.
fix: Do not use 1.0 for anything where inter-frame stability matters.
value: Version 1.0 shipped without a temporal layer because a code bug made the layer look like it destroyed lip-sync accuracy; the published paper carried that wrong claim. 1.5 adds the layer and the vendor reports significantly improved temporal consistency.

evidence: According to Fig.   11 , Wav2Lip has excellent lip-sync accuracy, but the generated videos are very blurry.
value: Best sync score in its cohort does not mean usable output. In LatentSync's HDTF comparison Wav2Lip scores Sync_conf 8.2 (highest of the four baselines) while posting the worst FID, 12.5. Sync metrics and visual fidelity move independently.

evidence: Our evaluation technique does not require ground-truth of any sorts. Given lip-synced videos we can directly calculate the scores from only the generated videos.
value: LSE-C / LSE-D, the metrics Wav2Lip introduced and that the whole field now quotes, are computed from the generated video alone with no reference. They therefore measure audio-lip agreement only and cannot register blur, identity loss, or box artifacts.

evidence: Experiment with the `--resize_factor` argument, to get a lower-resolution video. Why? The models are trained on faces that were at a lower resolution. You might get better, visually pleasing results for 720p videos than for 1080p videos (in many cases, the latter works well too).
fix: Use --resize_factor to downscale the input toward the training face resolution.
value: Source resolution above the training face resolution makes results worse, not better; 1080p often looks worse than 720p. The commercial HD variant still only synthesises a 192x288 face region.

evidence: If you see the mouth position dislocated or some weird artifacts such as two mouths, then it can be because of over-smoothing the face detections. Use the `--nosmooth` argument and give it another try.
fix: Pass --nosmooth; also adjust --pads (e.g. `--pads 0 20 0 0`) so the chin is inside the crop.
value: Named artifact class: dislocated mouth position and doubled mouths, caused by temporal smoothing of the face-detection boxes rather than by the generator.

evidence: - Identity preservation: Some details of the original face are not well preserved, such as mustache, lip shape and color.
value: Vendor's own LIMITATIONS section admits identity detail loss: mustache, lip shape and lip colour are not preserved from the source face.

evidence: - Jitter: There exists some jitter as the current pipeline adopts single-frame generation.
value: Visible jitter is structural, not tunable: the pipeline generates one frame at a time with no temporal module.

evidence: - Resolution: Though MuseTalk uses a face region size of 256 x 256, which make it better than other open-source methods, it has not yet reached the theoretical resolution bound.
fix: Apply GFPGAN or similar super-resolution after MuseTalk if higher resolution is needed.
value: Face region is fixed at 256x256; the vendor states this is below the resolution they consider achievable and recommends bolting on a super-resolution model.

evidence: Note: For optimal results, we recommend using input videos with 25fps, which is the same fps used during model training. If your video has a lower frame rate, you can use frame interpolation or convert it to 25fps using ffmpeg.
fix: Convert to 25 fps with ffmpeg or frame interpolation before inference.
value: Input frame rate other than 25 fps degrades results — 25 fps is the training rate.

evidence: However, we observed that an increased CFG results in pronounced wrinkles on the characters, whereas a decreased CFG compromises lip synchronization and motion expressiveness.
fix: CFG annealing — progressively reduce CFG magnitude across the denoising steps.
value: Classifier-free guidance is a two-sided failure axis: high CFG stamps pronounced wrinkles onto the character, low CFG breaks lip sync and flattens motion.

evidence: OmniHuman is capable of producing video segments of arbitrary length within memory constraints based on the provided reference images and various driving signals. To ensure temporal coherence and identity consistency in long videos, the last five frames of the previous segment are utilized as motion frames.
value: Long output is produced segment-by-segment with only the last five frames of the previous segment carried over as motion frames; length is bounded by memory, and identity consistency depends entirely on that five-frame handoff.

evidence: We investigated the impact of reference image ratios on the generation of 30-second videos ... revealing that a lower reference ratio leads to more pronounced error accumulation, characterized by increased noise and color shifts in the background, degrading performance.
fix: Train/infer with the reference-image ratio above the audio ratio.
value: Measured on 30-second generations: when the reference image is weighted below the audio condition, error accumulates as background noise and colour shifts, and reference identity is lost because audio dominates generation.

evidence: Figure 3: Quantitative comparisons with audio-conditioned portrait animation baselines.
value: CelebV-HQ Sync-C: OmniHuman 5.199, Loopy 4.849, Hallo 4.130, Hallo-3 3.933, SadTalker 3.843, EchoMimic 3.136, VExpress 3.547. FID: OmniHuman 31.435 vs VExpress 65.098. Even the leader sits well under real-video Sync-C (~7 in comparable Hallo2 tables).

evidence: A significant limitation of this method is the necessity to maintain minimal differences in appearance and motion across generated clips, which hampers substantial variations in lip movements, facial expressions, and poses, often resulting in blurriness and distorted expressions and postures due to the enforced continuity constraints.
fix: Patch-drop augmentation with Gaussian noise on the conditioning motion frames.
value: Incremental (motion-frame) long-video generation accumulates error in both face and background; parallel generation instead enforces continuity so hard that lip movement and expression range collapse into blur and distortion.

evidence: (1) Reliance on a single reference image constrains the diversity of generated expressions and poses, indicating a need for multiple references or advanced models capable of synthesizing varied facial features. (2) While the patch-drop data augmentation technique effectively preserves motion dynamics, it may introduce artifacts
value: Vendor-stated limits of the long-duration/4K method: a single reference image caps expression and pose diversity; the patch-drop augmentation that fixes drift can itself introduce artifacts; 4K generation is too compute-heavy for real time.

evidence: our method successfully handle long term consistency, circumventing identity similarity decrease in motion frames and mixed blurry texture in overlapping results.
fix: Time-aware position shift fusion instead of motion frames or overlap.
value: The two standard long-video stitching strategies fail in distinguishable ways: motion-frame conditioning loses identity similarity over time; latent overlap produces mixed blurry texture. Measured over 8-frame settings: motion frames Sync-C 2.465, overlap 2.544, shift-fusion 2.689.

evidence: we argue that this creates a critical artifact: the model learns a spurious correlation that the reference image should appear literally within the generated sequence, severely restricting motion dynamics and conflicting with the audio and text driving signals.
fix: Pseudo Last Frame — place the reference at the last-frame position with shifted positional encoding and drop it after rendering.
value: Reference-image identity conditioning is itself the cause of stiff output: the model learns the reference must appear literally in the generated frames, which restricts motion and fights the audio/text driving signal. Sampling references from outside the clip trades that for loss of content relevance.

evidence: However, as these objective metrics often fail to capture higher-level semantic qualities and overall perceptual realism, we also conducted a comprehensive subjective user study with 40 participants.
fix: Score defect rates (LSI/MU/ID) with human raters alongside the objective metrics.
value: ByteDance's own position: FID/FVD/IQA/ASE/Sync-C do not capture semantic quality or perceptual realism, so they ran a 40-participant study scoring explicit defect rates — Lip-sync Inconsistency, Motion Unnaturalness, Image Distortion.
